abstract: The transition from oocyte to embryo relies on the utilization of maternal macromolecules that accumulate during oogenesis. Change in phosphorylation status of maternal proteins is thought to drive developmental events during egg activation (EA) given that transcription does not occur during this time. To determine how mature oocytes acquire phosphorylation signatures on maternal proteins that are compatible with phospho-changes at EA, we analyzed phosphorylation dynamics during oocyte maturation (OM). We found widespread acquisition of phosphorylation at CDK1-MAPK sites during OM, and these sites were largely dephosphorylated during EA. We determined that the calcium-stimulated phosphatase Calcineurin is required for dephosphorylation of CDK1-MAPK substrates at EA; genetic perturbation of CDK1 or Calcineurin altered phosphorylation patterns at EA and induced precocious embryonic translation in oocytes. Ex vivo developmental assays revealed crosstalk between MAPK and CDK1 during OM: while depletion of either MAPK or CDK1 alone mildly impacts gross oocyte morphogenesis during OM, reducing the activity of both together dramatically reduced OM efficiency. Further, in MAPK-depleted conditions, CDK1 activity levels drastically increase in a temporally-sensitive manner, suggesting compensation for MAPK by CDK1 to ensure faithful establishment of maternal phospho-protein load. Finally, we show that the receipt of sperm during fertilization has no impact on phosphorylation events at EA. Our analyses connect the earliest events in embryonic initiation to the factors that keep oocytes arrested, providing novel insights as to the dynamics and mechanisms of maternal phospho-protein regulation during the transition from oogenesis to embryogenesis.
